adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py:56 — The asynchronous task applies its captured assignee without checking whether a newer assignment was queued, so out-of-order workers can overwrite the latest state in a linked system.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real architectural concern. The diff adds an AssignmentSource with a 'queued' timestamp field (line 17 in assignment_source.py), but the sync_assignee_outbound task at line 56 doesn't use this timestamp to check ordering before applying the assignment. The parsed_assignment_source is only used to check if should_sync should proceed (preventing cycles), not to verify temporal ordering. This is a valid concern about potential race conditions in distributed task processing, though it's more of a design limitation than a bug - the timestamp field exists but isn't used for ordering validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:141 — Every producer now sends a new Celery task keyword, so queued calls routed to pre-deploy workers will fail with an unexpected-keyword TypeError during a rolling deployment.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async is now called with a new keyword argument 'assignment_source_dict' (lines 137-143 in sync.py). The task function sync_assignee_outbound in sync_assignee_outbound.py is also modified to accept this new parameter. During a rolling deployment, if a producer (running new code) sends a task with 'assignment_source_dict' to a worker still running old code, the old worker's task function won't have this parameter and will raise a TypeError for the unexpected keyword argument. This is a real backward compatibility issue during rolling deployments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — queued uses an import-time datetime default, so every source created in a worker reports the same stale timestamp instead of its actual enqueue time

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default value in the dataclass definition at line 18. In Python, default values are evaluated once at class definition time (import time), not at instance creation time. This means all instances of AssignmentSource will share the same timestamp from when the module was first imported, rather than getting the actual time when each instance is created. This is a well-known Python gotcha with mutable/callable defaults.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:411 — The assignee-specific AssignmentSource was added to the unrelated sync_status_outbound abstraction even though no status path uses it, unnecessarily polluting every integration's status contract.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the `assignment_source` parameter was added to the `sync_status_outbound` abstract method signature (lines 408-417), but the diff shows this parameter is only used in the assignee sync path, not the status sync path. Looking at the diff, `AssignmentSource` is used in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, `sync_assignee_outbound` task, and the `should_sync` method for assignee operations. The status outbound method now has this parameter in its signature but there's no evidence in the diff that any status-related code path uses it. This is a legitimate architectural concern - adding an assignee-specific concept to an unrelated status abstraction creates unnecessary coupling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/models/groupassignee.py:13 — The core GroupAssignee model now depends directly on an integrations-service DTO, reversing the existing model-to-integration boundary and making assignment persistence coupled to one synchronization implementation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the GroupAssignee model (a core model in src/sentry/models/) now imports and uses AssignmentSource from src/sentry/integrations/services/. This creates a dependency from the core models layer to the integrations services layer. Looking at the diff, line 13 shows 'from sentry.integrations.services.assignment_source import AssignmentSource' being added to groupassignee.py, and the assign/deassign methods now accept assignment_source parameters of type AssignmentSource. This is a legitimate architectural concern about coupling direction - core models typically shouldn't depend on integration-specific DTOs. However, this is a design/architecture concern rather than a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:17 — timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import, so every source that omits `queued` carries the worker-start timestamp instead of its actual enqueue time.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a Python gotcha. In the dataclass definition at line 17, `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` uses a mutable default that is evaluated once at class definition time (module import), not at instance creation time. This means all AssignmentSource instances that don't explicitly provide a `queued` value will share the same timestamp from when the module was first imported. This is a real bug that would cause incorrect timestamps.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:166 — Add a two-integration test proving an inbound assignment skips its source while still syncing to a different linked integration, since the current single-integration test can pass even if all sourced updates are suppressed.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a gap in test coverage. The new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only tests that an assignment from integration A doesn't sync back to integration A. However, the code comment at line 385-387 states 'This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward.' There's no test verifying that when integration A triggers an assignment, it still syncs to integration B (a different linked integration). This is a valid test coverage concern for the new sync-cycle prevention logic, though it's a suggestion for additional coverage rather than a critical defect.
